question.prompt:
Suppose that \(13\) cards numbered \(1,\) \(2,\) \(3,\) \(\cdots,\) \(13\) are arranged in a row. The task is to pick them up in numerically increasing order, working repeatedly from left to right. In the example below, cards \(1,\) \(2,\) \(3\) are picked up on the first pass, \(4\) and \(5\) on the second pass, \(6\) on the third pass, \(7,\) \(8,\) \(9,\) \(10\) on the fourth pass, and \(11,\) \(12,\) \(13\) on the fifth pass. For how many of the \(13!\) possible orderings of the cards will the \(13\) cards be picked up in exactly two passes?

[Figure 1](figures/2022_AMC_10A_Q22_official_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
Within a pass, the cards we collect must appear from left to right in increasing numerical order. Once we know their positions, their order is forced. We can use this to count choices of positions instead of counting arbitrary rows.

If exactly two passes are needed, the first picks up \(1,2,\ldots,m\) for some \(1\le m\le12\). The second picks up \(m+1,m+2,\ldots,13\). Each of these two groups must already appear in increasing order in the row.

Try the construction with five cards. Mark positions \(2,4,5\) for the first group. There are three marked positions, so fill them, from left to right, with \(1,2,3\). Fill the other positions with \(4,5\), also in order. The row becomes

\[
4,\ 1,\ 5,\ 2,\ 3.
\]

On the first pass we collect \(1,2,3\). We have already passed \(4\), so we return to the left and collect \(4,5\) on a second pass. Notice that the marks specify positions, not card numbers.

For \(13\) cards, mark any selection of positions. If there are \(m\) marks, fill the marked positions with \(1,2,\ldots,m\), and the others with \(m+1,m+2,\ldots,13\), each group in increasing order. Every position has two independent choices, marked or unmarked, so there are \(2^{13}\) marking patterns. We temporarily allow no marks or all positions marked to keep this count simple.

Some patterns give a row needing only one pass. A one-pass row must be \(1,2,\ldots,13\), and our construction produces this row exactly when the marks occupy the first \(m\) positions. There are \(14\) such patterns, one for each \(m=0,1,\ldots,13\). We subtract \(14\), even though they all produce the same sorted row, because \(2^{13}\) counts marking patterns.

For every other pattern, an unmarked position lies before a marked position. Thus the first unmarked position, holding \(m+1\), lies to the left of the last marked position, holding \(m\). The first pass picks up \(1\) through \(m\), but by then has already passed \(m+1\). The remaining cards are in increasing order, so a second pass picks them all up.

There is no double counting among these two-pass rows. A row's actual first pass tells us exactly which positions were marked. Conversely, every two-pass row comes from marking those positions. The required count is therefore

\[
2^{13}-14=8192-14=\boxed{8178},
\]

which is D.

The clue here is that each group has a fixed internal order. In such problems, try choosing the positions occupied by a group. Then check which choices really give the required behavior and whether the finished arrangement uniquely determines your choices.
solutions.title: Encode two ordered card groups by marked positions and remove sorted-row patterns.
